                         Ayda Shahriari1, Mohsen Mohammadi1
                1 Marine Additive Manufacturing Centre of Excellence (MAMCE)/ University of New Brunswick
                                15 Dineen Drive, Fredericton, NB, Canada
                                  [email redacted]; [email redacted]


Extended Abstract
    Additive Manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a transformative metal production technology that enables the direct
fabrication of complex components. Unlike traditional metal processing methods, AM utilizes laser or electron beams to melt
metal powders and build parts layer by layer. Additionally, the wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) method employs
a wire as the input material, undergoing fusion and placement onto a substrate. This design flexibility and the ability to
produce intricate geometries have made AM a promising manufacturing approach across various industries [1].
   The production of copper-based alloys, particularly Nickel-Aluminium Bronze (NAB), using WAAM and Laser Powder
Bed Fusion (LPBF) techniques, has been extensively investigated in our research group as well as in the literature [2], [3],
[4]. It is well established that variations in AM processes significantly influence defect formation and the microstructural
features of metallic components. Factors such as preheating of the substrate/platform, along with the geometry of the
fabricated components, affect thermal conditions during the AM process. Consequently, these variations lead to different
microstructural evolutions, which are closely correlated with the functional performance of the components, especially their
corrosion resistance.
   The objective of this study is to investigate the correlation between the microstructural features of NAB components
fabricated using WAAM and LPBF techniques and their corresponding corrosion resistance.
   NAB samples were manufactured using gas metal arc welding (GMAW) within the WAAM process, resulting in
components referred to as WAAM-NAB. These components were produced in both cuboidal and cylindrical shapes.
Similarly, the LPBF method was employed to fabricate NAB components using gas-atomized powder with a nominal
chemical composition of Al: 8.5-9.5 wt.%, Ni: 4-5 wt.%, Fe: 3.4-4.5 wt.%, Mn: 0.8-1.5 wt.%, with copper as the balance
element. Both cuboidal and cylindrical samples were fabricated using the LPBF process.
    Electrochemical measurements were conducted on the AM samples in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution to evaluate their
corrosion performance. Potentiodynamic polarization  tests and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were
employed to assess the corrosion behaviour. Microstructural analyses were performed using various characterization
techniques, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), to gain insights into
the effects of microstructural features on corrosion performance.
   The results revealed that the formation of martensitic phases and the precipitation of kappa phases, coupled with finer
grain sizes in LPBF components compared to WAAM components, led to a reduction in their corrosion resistance. WAAM-
fabricated NAB components predominantly consisted of the α-phase and kappa phases, which provided superior corrosion
resistance compared to their LPBF counterparts. Furthermore, changing the geometry of LPBF components from cuboidal
to cylindrical shapes did not significantly affect their microstructure or corrosion characteristics. However, this phenomenon
exhibited an inverse trend in the WAAM-fabricated components, where shape variations between cuboidal and cylindrical
samples resulted in noticeable differences in corrosion resistance.
    These findings highlight the significant influence of AM processing parameters and component geometry on the
microstructural features and corrosion resistance of NAB components, providing valuable insights for optimizing AM
techniques for enhanced performance in marine and other corrosive environments.

Abstract:
Laser Hot Wire (LHW) Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Additive Manufacturing (AM) processes are capable of manufacturing parts with a high deposition rate. There is a growing research interest in replacing large cast Nickel Aluminum Bronze (NAB) components using LHW DED processes for maritime applications. Understanding thermomechanical behavior during LHW DED of NAB is a critical step towards the production of high-quality NAB parts with desired performance and properties. In this paper, finite element simulations are first used to predict the thermomechanical time histories during LHW DED of NAB test coupons with an increasing geometric complexity, including single-layer and multilayer depositions. Simulation results are experimentally validated through in situ measurements of temperatures at multiple locations in the substrate as well as displacement at the free end of the substrate during and immediately following the deposition process. The results in this paper demonstrate that the finite element predictions have good agreement with the experimental measurements of both temperature and distortion history. The maximum prediction error for temperature is 5% for single-layer samples and 6% for multilayer samples, while the distortion prediction error is about 12% for single-layer samples and less than 4% for multilayer samples. In addition, this study shows the effectiveness of including a stress relaxation temperature at 500 °C during FE modeling to allow for better prediction of the low cross-layer accumulation of distortion in multilayer deposition of NAB.

Abstract:
Purpose
This study aims to investigate the scientific impact of additive manufacturing in recent years, considering its evolution as an Industry 4.0 technology and also in the current context of Industry 5.0. For this aim, advanced statistics and scientometric tools have been used.

Design/methodology/approach
This study aims to explore the trends and impacts of additive manufacturing, focusing on its evolution and its relationship with Industry 4.0 and 5.0. For this purpose, a scientometric study and a meta-analysis of data extracted from the scientific Scopus database have been carried out. R programming and specific bibliometric software have been used to conduct the research. Initially, the data were evaluated from various perspectives, including sources, topics and impact indexes, to assess trends derived from the volume of publications, the impact of sources and affiliations, as well as the production segmented by country and the relationships between authors from different countries. Subsequently, a meta-analysis on keywords has been carried out using two distinct clustering methodologies: link strength and fractionalization. The results obtained were compared to establish a specific taxonomy of the AM subtopics, considering AM as a single body of knowledge related to Industries 4.0 and 5.0 paradigms. The analyses carried out have shown the impact and strong evolution of additive manufacturing as a field of knowledge at the world level, both from the point of view of manufacturing processes and from the point of view of materials science. In addition, some differences have been detected depending on the country. As a result of the meta-analysis, four different subtopics have been detected, some of which are highly related to other technologies and approaches in Industries 4.0 and 5.0 paradigms. Additionally, it establishes a comprehensive taxonomy for AM research, serving as a foundational reference for future studies aimed at exploring the evolution and transformative impact of this technology.

Findings
The analyses carried out have shown the impact and strong evolution of additive manufacturing as a field of knowledge at the world level, both from the point of view of manufacturing processes and from the point of view of materials science. In addition, some differences have been detected depending on the country. As a result of the meta-analysis, four different subtopics have been detected: one of them directly related to the use of recently developed Industry 4.0 technologies in additive manufacturing. The results provide a starting point for prospective studies to understand the evolution and disruption of this technology.

Originality/value
The paper is original and is based on data systematically extracted from scientific databases. Then, a specific methodology based on different advanced tools was applied for scientometric evaluation and meta-analysis.

{"answer": "# Ultrasonic atomization of nickel–aluminium bronze: published precedent

**Yes.** Müller and co-workers reported recycling aluminium-bronze grinding chips by ultrasonic atomization for laser directed-energy deposition (DED) in 2023. A subsequent, accessible study by Uhlmann *et al.* (2024) identifies the chips as **nickel–aluminium bronze CuAl10Ni5Fe5, EN CC333G**, and gives measured properties of ultrasonically atomized powder made from those chips. The 2024 authors describe the 2023 work as using powder from the same grinding chips to produce DED specimens. The 2023 paper itself could not be examined here, so its apparatus settings and results should **not** be assumed identical to those reported in 2024. The accessible experiment identifies an **AMAZEMET AUS 500 Atomizer**, not a rePOWDER unit. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000027)

## Direct NAB report: Uhlmann *et al.* (2024)

| Requested item | Documented result |
|---|---|
| Feedstock | Grinding chips collected during ship-propeller manufacture; CuAl10Ni5Fe5 (CC333G). A 125 µm sieve was used to prepare raw-chip material for some analyses. No separate cleaning protocol is specified. (pqac-00000028) |
| Atomizer; melt delivery | AMAZEMET/BluePower **AUS 500**; induction heating to **1300 °C**; melt delivered through a nozzle system at **1.5 bar**. The paper does not specify whether this pressure is gauge or absolute. (pqac-00000027) |
| Crucible; nozzle; vibrating plate | **Crucible and nozzle materials not reported.** The vibrating sonotrode/plate is described as **binder-free woven carbon fibre**. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000022) |
| Frequency; amplitude | **40 kHz**; amplitude **not reported**. (pqac-00000027) |
| Atmosphere; chamber oxygen | **Argon grade 5.0** during melting and atomization. A measured chamber oxygen concentration is **not reported**; the gas grade is not such a measurement. (pqac-00000027) |
| Powder yield; sizing | Atomization mass yield and usable-size-fraction yield **not reported**. Powder was sieved through **200 µm mesh** to remove spatters. Dynamic-image-analysis **area-equivalent-diameter** percentiles, Xₐ,₁₀/Xₐ,₅₀/Xₐ,₉₀, were **48/98/174 µm**; these are not laser-diffraction D-values. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000031) |
| Morphology and defects | Predominantly spherical: mean two-dimensional aspect ratio **0.935**, with **82%** of particles having aspect ratio >0.9. A limited number of satellites and agglomerates occurred, but fewer than in the study’s commercial gas-atomized comparator. Spatters and fine carbon fibres up to approximately **20 µm** were observed; virtually no internal gas inclusions were seen in examined powder cross-sections. No retained chip-shaped particles were observed after remelting. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032) |
| Powder oxygen | **0.013 wt.% O (approximately 130 ppm by mass)**, measured by hot-gas extraction; the sieved chips contained **0.073 wt.% (730 ppm)**. The figure labels can be misread: the accompanying text identifies the ultrasonically atomized powder as having the *lowest* measured oxygen, assigning **0.019 wt.%** to the commercial gas-atomized comparator. These are **powder** measurements, not chamber oxygen levels. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000033) |
| Other process problems | The authors identify fibres shed from the hot sonotrode and residual ceramic grinding-abrasive contaminants (ZrO₂, Al₂O₃ or SiO₂); the ultrasonic powder contained fewer abrasive particles than mechanically milled samples. **No nozzle clogging, quantified plate wear, interrupted melt flow, or atomization interruption is documented** in the accessible report. Its warning about possible *DED powder-feed-nozzle* clogging concerns the **ball-milled comparator**, not the ultrasonic atomizer. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026) |

The ultrasonic powder’s Carney-funnel time was **8.62 s/150 g**, angle of repose **13.74°**, and Hausner ratio **1.05**, versus **10.55 s/150 g**, **20.08°**, and **1.12** for the commercial comparator. That comparator is **CuAl9.5Fe, not nickel–aluminium bronze**; its properties should not be presented as a gas-atomized NAB control. The 2024 authors assessed powder suitability but said actual DED powder-feeding and deposited-part properties required further testing. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029)

## Related Cu–Al ultrasonic experiment, not bronze

Singh *et al.* (2026) atomized **Al–33 wt.% Cu**, an **Al-rich** alloy rather than Cu-rich aluminium bronze, using an AMAZEMET system. High-purity elemental feedstocks were melted in a **boron-nitride-coated graphite crucible**, held at **800 °C for five minutes**, and fed onto a **carbon-fibre-composite plate** attached to a **60 kHz** sonotrode. Argon purges were used; the authors describe a pressure ramp from **150 to 850 mbar over 50 s** to control melt flow. Their accessible extended abstract gives **no powder PSD, morphology, oxygen content, atomizer setup or powder yield**. (pqac-00000041)
- **Powder-fed laser DED:** Saai *et al.* (2025) document **30 kg of gas-atomized NAB powder** for one ship-propeller-hub repair, specifying Cu **79–83.2**, Al **8.5–9.5**, Ni **4–5**, Fe **3.5–4.5**, Mn **0.8–1.5 wt.%**, with minor Si and Pb limits. They report **77% of supplied powder deposited** and **23% overspray**. This is **DED deposition efficiency, not gas- or ultrasonic-atomization yield**; powder PSD and oxygen are not supplied. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000007)
- **NAB powder characterization outside laser AM:** Krebs (2016) reports **CuAl10Fe5Ni5** made by electrode-induction-melting **gas atomization in nitrogen** for thermal/cold spraying. As-atomized batches have approximately **d₁₀/d₅₀/d₉₀ = 19/31/48 to 23/36/59 µm**, **350 ± 20 ppm O**, and nearly spherical particles with few satellites. These are useful powder-production benchmarks, **not proof that these particular batches were used for LPBF or DED**. (pqac-00000005)

**Bottom line:** There is a direct, quantitatively characterized **ultrasonically atomized NAB** precedent on the AUS 500. The available publication supports its temperature, delivery pressure, carbon-fibre sonotrode, frequency, argon grade and powder properties, but leaves **crucible/nozzle materials, amplitude, measured chamber oxygen, mass yield and operating interruptions unresolved**. The cited 2023 predecessor may contain further information, but its full text was unavailable for verification. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000030)

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide evidence of an actual ultrasonic-atomization experiment on aluminium-bronze or nickel-aluminium-bronze chips, nor does it report the requested ultrasonic-process parameters such as melt temperature, crucible, nozzle, sonotrode material, frequency, amplitude, argon/oxygen conditions, yield, or atomization problems. Instead, it describes conventionally gas-atomized bronze powders used for thermal and kinetic spraying. Nickel-aluminium bronze (CuAl10Fe5Ni5/NAB) powders were produced by electrode induction-melting gas atomization in nitrogen. Reported NAB batches had particle-size distributions broadly within d10 = 19–28 µm, d50 = 30–38 µm, and d90 = 45–59 µm, with oxygen contents of approximately 350–410 ppm depending on batch and annealing state. The powders had good flowability (17–27 s/50 g), apparent densities of 55–60%, and mostly spherical particles with few satellites and fines. As-atomized NAB contained dendritic, grain-refined, and martensitic structures; martensite was considered detrimental to deformability. Annealing at 600 °C reduced martensite, with 7 h producing a martensite-free state and more homogeneous microstructure. These data may serve as background for gas-atomized NAB feedstock, but they should not be attributed to the 2023 ultrasonic chip-recycling experiment.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide an explicit reference to ultrasonic atomization of aluminum bronze, Cu-Al alloy powders, or a 2023 Müller experiment. It describes a study on Ni-Al-bronze powder used to produce cavitation-resistant coatings on GL-A shipbuilding steel, using warm spraying and HVOF spraying rather than ultrasonic atomization. Warm spraying controls particle velocity and temperature through nitrogen flow rate, combustion pressure, nozzle geometry, stand-off distance, and substrate preheating; particles are thermally softened and may be molten or semi-molten before impact. HVOF uses combustion of a gaseous fuel with oxygen to heat and accelerate powder, with adjustable oxygen-to-fuel ratio, cooling gas, spray distance, and other parameters. The cited experiments involve simulated particle velocities and temperatures and coating formation, not atomization of a melt. The excerpt therefore cannot establish the methodology of Müller (2023), nor verify claims concerning the 2026 Singh study on Al-based powders or Cu alloys. Conceptually, ultrasonic atomization would refer to producing droplets or powder from a liquid metal using ultrasonic excitation, whereas ultrasound-assisted melting concerns applying ultrasound to a molten alloy to influence phenomena such as melt treatment, degassing, dispersion, or solidification. Cavitation erosion is a service or testing phenomenon involving damaging bubble collapse at a coated surface; it is distinct from acoustic cavitation used during ultrasonic melt processing.

Its powder-production reference is instead the EIGA process for Ni-Al-bronze, a Cu-Al-Ni-Fe alloy powder. The discussion focuses on cold-gas-sprayed coatings and their cavitation-erosion performance, not on powder atomization methodology. It reports that the powder contains an alpha matrix, beta1 martensitic structures, and iron- and nickel-rich kappa precipitates. EIGA is said to produce high cooling rates and metastable beta phases that transform into martensite; approximately 10–15 at% martensite was measured in the hard NAB particles. Martensite increases powder strength, restricts particle deformability, raises critical bonding conditions, and contributes to scatter in coating properties. The excerpt therefore provides potentially useful alloy and powder-microstructure context, but it does not establish ultrasonic atomization, ultrasound-assisted melting, or ultrasound-induced cavitation during processing. Its use of “cavitation” concerns erosion testing of deposited coatings: stronger, harder, more conductive, and less porous coatings show lower cavitation erosion rates. Accordingly, the passage cannot verify the methodology of a cited Müller (2023) study or distinguish ultrasonic atomization from ultrasound-assisted melt treatment beyond showing that the present work used EIGA and evaluated cavitation resistance after cold spraying.

snippets: Ultrasonic atomization (UA) is an attractive manufacturing method for both lab-scale alloy development and scalable powder production.
The molten stream impinged upon a carbon fiber composite (CFC) plate attached to a 60 kHz sonotrode.
The typical atomization yield in the sub-300 µm size range was approximately 80–90% by weight.
Representative alloy compositions included pure Al (control), Al–33Cu (33 wt.% Cu), Al–13Si (13 wt.% Si), and Al–33Mg (33 wt.% Mg).
These compositions were selected near their respective eutectic points to promote the formation of alternating lamellar microstructures.

UA also enables composition-sensitive solidification, producing spherical powders with microstructures—such as eutectic/lamellar, dendritic, or segregated skins—that can be tailored to influence oxidation behavior.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial process and characterization data, but not the complete dataset requested. Aluminium bronze grinding chips were processed by ultrasonic atomization using an AMAZEMET AUS 500 Atomizer (AMAZEMET Sp. z o.o. and BluePower Casting Systems GmbH). The feedstock was heated to 1300 °C, delivered through a nozzle at 1.5 bar onto a carbon-fiber sonotrode operating at 40 kHz, and atomized under argon grade 5.0. The atomized powder was passed through a 200 µm sieve to remove spatters. During milling, an unspecified measure was used to reduce oxidation; the excerpt gives no detailed chip-cleaning protocol, crucible or nozzle material, sonotrode amplitude, oxygen concentration in ppm or volume percent, atomization yield, or fraction yields. Particle size was measured by dynamic image analysis according to ISO 13322-2. The gas-atomized reference powder had XA,10 = 64 µm and XA,90 = 135 µm. Ball-milled BM-1 and BM-2 had XA,10–XA,90 ranges of 66–254 µm and 54–235 µm, respectively. Impact-whirl-milled IWM-2 measured 72–155 µm and was closer to the gas-atomized reference. contexts.context: This excerpt contains the paper’s concluding comparative data, but not the requested full process table or all precise atomization details. The study compares recycled nickel aluminium bronze grinding-chip feedstocks produced by mechanical comminution, ultrasonic atomization, and re-melting for additive manufacturing. Ultrasonic atomization generated highly spherical, flowable powder with Hausner ratio H = 1.05. Ball milling reduced chip size but produced unfavorable morphology, with mean aspect ratio ARmean = 0.576, oxygen content O = 0.19%, and H = 1.29. Higher-speed impact whirl milling produced more rounded and reduced particles, with ARmean = 0.633 and H = 1.21; IWM-2 was reported as the most favorable mechanically comminuted material. Mechanical-milling samples showed noticeable ceramic-abrasive contamination from grinding belts, while ultrasonic-atomized material contained substantially less abrasive contamination but had a few carbon-fiber impurities attributed to the sonotrode. The authors state that these contaminants can impair powder quality and cause defects in manufactured parts. Ultrasonic-atomized and impact-whirl-milled powders appeared suitable for laser-based directed energy deposition (DED-LB), but further testing was required under actual powder-feeding conditions and to assess the mechanical properties of deposited structures. snippets: Ultrasonic atomization produced highly spherical and flowable powder (H = 1.05)
Ball milling reduced the particle size of the chips but resulted in a high O (0.19%) and an unfavorable morphology (ARmean = 0.576), negatively impacting flowability (H = 1.29).
Impact whirl milling, with sufficient rotation speeds, produced chip powders with promising properties in terms of morphology (ARmean = 0.633) and flowability (H = 1.21).
Contaminations with ceramic abrasives from the grinding process and carbon fibers from the sonotrode used in ultrasonic atomization were found in the produced powders.
In particular, the powders from ultrasonic atomization and impact whirl milling appear well-suited for the DED-LB process.

contexts.context: A 2024 *Materials* study reports ultrasonic atomization of ship-propeller nickel aluminum bronze CuAl10Ni5Fe5 (CC333G), closely related to UNS C95800/C63000. Chips were produced by grinding and sieved at 125 µm. An AMAZEMET/BluePower AUS 500 atomizer was used; the listed sonotrode frequency was 40 kHz. The study compares this ultrasonic powder (UA) with commercial gas-atomized CuAl9.5Fe (Oerlikon Metco 51NS). The excerpt does not yet provide melt temperature, crucible/nozzle/plate materials, amplitude, atmosphere/oxygen, yield, PSD, morphology, oxygen content, or operational problems.
contexts.question:
Has anyone ultrasonically atomized nickel aluminum bronze or aluminum bronze (UNS C63000, C95800,
C95500, CuAl10Ni5Fe4, CuAl10Fe3 and similar), for example in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another
ultrasonic atomizer? For each report give the feedstock, melt temperature, crucible, nozzle and plate
(sonotrode) materials, frequency and amplitude, atmosphere and oxygen level, yield, particle size
distribution, morphology (satellites, flakes, irregular particles), oxygen content, and any problems
such as nozzle clogging, plate wear or interrupted flow. If there are none, give the closest
precedents: ultrasonic atomization of other aluminum-containing copper alloys, and gas atomization of
nickel aluminum bronze powder for laser powder-bed fusion or directed energy deposition.

contexts.context: A 2024 study examined ultrasonic-atomized powder (UA) from CuAl10Fe5Ni5 (nickel aluminum bronze), alongside gas-atomized CuAl9.5Fe. UA had the lowest oxygen, approximately 0.019%, versus 0.013% for gas-atomized reference and 0.119–0.190% for milled powders, attributed to effective shielding. Its Carney flow rate was 8.62 s/150 g, better than gas atomization (10.55). SEM found isolated spatters and carbon fibers up to approximately 20 µm, likely shed from a binder-free woven-carbon sonotrode; possible effects include porosity or lack of fusion. No process settings, PSD, yield, temperatures, nozzle/plate details, or clogging/wear data appear.

contexts.context: The 2024 study processed aluminum-bronze CC333G (nominal Cu 76–83%, Al 8.5–10.5%, Fe 4–5.5%, Ni 4–6%, Mn ≤3%) by ultrasonic atomization (UA), alongside gas-atomized reference powder (GA). UA particles were predominantly spherical: mean aspect ratio 0.94, with 82% having AR > 0.9, substantially fewer satellites/agglomerates than GA, and almost no gas inclusions. Composition was Cu 75.16%, Al 9.83%, Fe 6.76%, Ni 5.91%, Mn 2.33%. Ceramic contamination (ZrO₂, Al₂O₃, SiO₂) was limited. The excerpt gives no melt temperature, crucible/nozzle/sonotrode materials, frequency, amplitude, atmosphere/O₂, yield, PSD, oxygen assay, or operational problems.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports ultrasonic atomization of CuAl10Fe5Ni5 (nickel aluminum bronze), compared with gas-atomized CuAl9.5Fe and milled material. Ultrasonic powder was highly spherical, with minimal agglomerates/satellites, and had excellent flow: angle of repose 13.74° versus gas-atomized 20.08°, and Hausner ratio 1.05 versus 1.12. Milled powders were less flowable (AOR 29.09–35.15°, Hausner 1.21–1.35) and had elevated oxygen, potentially causing insufficient feeding and nozzle clogging in DED-LB. This excerpt provides no atomizer operating parameters, oxygen level, yield, PSD, melt temperature, crucible/nozzle/plate materials, frequency, amplitude, or wear/clogging observations for the ultrasonic run.

contexts.context: A 2024 study atomized recycled aluminum-bronze chips using an AMAZEMET/BluePower AUS 500. Feedstock was heated to 1300 °C in an induction furnace and delivered at 1.5 bar onto a carbon-fiber sonotrode (“plate”) vibrating at 40 kHz; argon grade 5.0 was used for melting and atomization. Spatters were removed through a 200 µm sieve. The excerpt gives no amplitude, crucible/nozzle materials, oxygen concentration, yield, oxygen content, clogging/wear observations, or morphology results. PSD/morphology were measured by ISO 13322-2 dynamic image analysis; later text indicates the ultrasonic-atomized PSD discussion continues beyond the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt is only a reference list and reports no experimental parameters or results for ultrasonic atomization of nickel/aluminum bronze. Relevant precedents cited are Lierke and Grießhammer, “Formation of Metal Powders by Ultrasonic Atomization of Molten Metals” (1967), and [name redacted] et al., “Novel Cold Crucible Ultrasonic Atomization Powder Production Method for 3D Printing” (2021). Most directly relevant is Müller et al. (2023), “Using Ultrasonic Atomization to Recycle Aluminium Bronze Chips for Additive Laser Directed Energy Deposition.” Additional Müller publications (2021, 2022) concern recycling aluminum-bronze grinding waste, not necessarily atomization. No frequencies, temperatures, materials, yields, PSDs, oxygen data, or failure observations appear.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone ultrasonically atomized nickel aluminum bronze or aluminum bronze (UNS C63000, C95800,
C95500, CuAl10Ni5Fe4, CuAl10Fe3 and similar), for example in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another
ultrasonic atomizer? For each report give the feedstock, melt temperature, crucible, nozzle and plate
(sonotrode) materials, frequency and amplitude, atmosphere and oxygen level, yield, particle size
distribution, morphology (satellites, flakes, irregular particles), oxygen content, and any problems
such as nozzle clogging, plate wear or interrupted flow. If there are none, give the closest
precedents: ultrasonic atomization of other aluminum-containing copper alloys, and gas atomization of
nickel aluminum bronze powder for laser powder-bed fusion or directed energy deposition.


Yes. # Ultrasonic atomization of nickel–aluminium bronze: published precedent

**Yes.** Müller and co-workers reported recycling aluminium-bronze grinding chips by ultrasonic atomization for laser directed-energy deposition (DED) in 2023. A subsequent, accessible study by Uhlmann *et al.* (2024) identifies the chips as **nickel–aluminium bronze CuAl10Ni5Fe5, EN CC333G**, and gives measured properties of ultrasonically atomized powder made from those chips. The 2024 authors describe the 2023 work as using powder from the same grinding chips to produce DED specimens. The 2023 paper itself could not be examined here, so its apparatus settings and results should **not** be assumed identical to those reported in 2024. The accessible experiment identifies an **AMAZEMET AUS 500 Atomizer**, not a rePOWDER unit. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 2-4, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 15-15, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6)

## Direct NAB report: Uhlmann *et al.* (2024)

| Requested item | Documented result |
|---|---|
| Feedstock | Grinding chips collected during ship-propeller manufacture; CuAl10Ni5Fe5 (CC333G). A 125 µm sieve was used to prepare raw-chip material for some analyses. No separate cleaning protocol is specified. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 2-4) |
| Atomizer; melt delivery | AMAZEMET/BluePower **AUS 500**; induction heating to **1300 °C**; melt delivered through a nozzle system at **1.5 bar**. The paper does not specify whether this pressure is gauge or absolute. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6) |
| Crucible; nozzle; vibrating plate | **Crucible and nozzle materials not reported.** The vibrating sonotrode/plate is described as **binder-free woven carbon fibre**. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 10-12) |
| Frequency; amplitude | **40 kHz**; amplitude **not reported**. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6) |
| Atmosphere; chamber oxygen | **Argon grade 5.0** during melting and atomization. A measured chamber oxygen concentration is **not reported**; the gas grade is not such a measurement. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6) |
| Powder yield; sizing | Atomization mass yield and usable-size-fraction yield **not reported**. Powder was sieved through **200 µm mesh** to remove spatters. Dynamic-image-analysis **area-equivalent-diameter** percentiles, Xₐ,₁₀/Xₐ,₅₀/Xₐ,₉₀, were **48/98/174 µm**; these are not laser-diffraction D-values. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 6-7, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation media 7cacbeef) |
| Morphology and defects | Predominantly spherical: mean two-dimensional aspect ratio **0.935**, with **82%** of particles having aspect ratio >0.9. A limited number of satellites and agglomerates occurred, but fewer than in the study’s commercial gas-atomized comparator. Spatters and fine carbon fibres up to approximately **20 µm** were observed; virtually no internal gas inclusions were seen in examined powder cross-sections. No retained chip-shaped particles were observed after remelting. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 6-7, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 7-10, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 10-12, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation media 2cf5986d) |
| Powder oxygen | **0.013 wt.% O (approximately 130 ppm by mass)**, measured by hot-gas extraction; the sieved chips contained **0.073 wt.% (730 ppm)**. The figure labels can be misread: the accompanying text identifies the ultrasonically atomized powder as having the *lowest* measured oxygen, assigning **0.019 wt.%** to the commercial gas-atomized comparator. These are **powder** measurements, not chamber oxygen levels. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 10-12, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation media 57b1d664) |
| Other process problems | The authors identify fibres shed from the hot sonotrode and residual ceramic grinding-abrasive contaminants (ZrO₂, Al₂O₃ or SiO₂); the ultrasonic powder contained fewer abrasive particles than mechanically milled samples. **No nozzle clogging, quantified plate wear, interrupted melt flow, or atomization interruption is documented** in the accessible report. Its warning about possible *DED powder-feed-nozzle* clogging concerns the **ball-milled comparator**, not the ultrasonic atomizer. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 10-12, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 7-10, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 12-13) |

The ultrasonic powder’s Carney-funnel time was **8.62 s/150 g**, angle of repose **13.74°**, and Hausner ratio **1.05**, versus **10.55 s/150 g**, **20.08°**, and **1.12** for the commercial comparator. That comparator is **CuAl9.5Fe, not nickel–aluminium bronze**; its properties should not be presented as a gas-atomized NAB control. The 2024 authors assessed powder suitability but said actual DED powder-feeding and deposited-part properties required further testing. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 2-4, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 10-12, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 12-13, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 13-15)

## Related Cu–Al ultrasonic experiment, not bronze

Singh *et al.* (2026) atomized **Al–33 wt.% Cu**, an **Al-rich** alloy rather than Cu-rich aluminium bronze, using an AMAZEMET system. High-purity elemental feedstocks were melted in a **boron-nitride-coated graphite crucible**, held at **800 °C for five minutes**, and fed onto a **carbon-fibre-composite plate** attached to a **60 kHz** sonotrode. Argon purges were used; the authors describe a pressure ramp from **150 to 850 mbar over 50 s** to control melt flow. They report **80–90 wt.% yield below 300 µm**, with size percentiles **45/91/194 µm** after removal of particles and flakes above 300 µm. Initial spattering occurred before the plate wetted, after which atomization stabilized. **Amplitude, nozzle material, measured chamber oxygen, powder oxygen concentration, and plate-wear rate are not given.** This experiment cannot establish a yield or safe operating window for Cu-rich NAB at 1300 °C. (singh2026synthesisandcharacterization pages 1-3, singh2026synthesisandcharacterization pages 3-7)

## Gas-atomized NAB precedents for laser AM

- **Laser powder-bed fusion:** Shahriari and Mohammadi (2025) explicitly report LPBF specimens made from **gas-atomized NAB powder**: Al **8.5–9.5**, Ni **4–5**, Fe **3.4–4.5**, Mn **0.8–1.5 wt.%**, balance Cu. Their accessible extended abstract gives **no powder PSD, morphology, oxygen content, atomizer setup or powder yield**. (shahriari2025additivelymanufacturednickelaluminium pages 1-2)
- **Powder-fed laser DED:** Saai *et al.* (2025) document **30 kg of gas-atomized NAB powder** for one ship-propeller-hub repair, specifying Cu **79–83.2**, Al **8.5–9.5**, Ni **4–5**, Fe **3.5–4.5**, Mn **0.8–1.5 wt.%**, with minor Si and Pb limits. They report **77% of supplied powder deposited** and **23% overspray**. This is **DED deposition efficiency, not gas- or ultrasonic-atomization yield**; powder PSD and oxygen are not supplied. (saai2025comparativelifecycle pages 6-8, saai2025comparativelifecycle pages 4-6)
- **NAB powder characterization outside laser AM:** Krebs (2016) reports **CuAl10Fe5Ni5** made by electrode-induction-melting **gas atomization in nitrogen** for thermal/cold spraying. As-atomized batches have approximately **d₁₀/d₅₀/d₉₀ = 19/31/48 to 23/36/59 µm**, **350 ± 20 ppm O**, and nearly spherical particles with few satellites. These are useful powder-production benchmarks, **not proof that these particular batches were used for LPBF or DED**. (krebs2016thermischesundkinetisches pages 40-43)

**Bottom line:** There is a direct, quantitatively characterized **ultrasonically atomized NAB** precedent on the AUS 500. The available publication supports its temperature, delivery pressure, carbon-fibre sonotrode, frequency, argon grade and powder properties, but leaves **crucible/nozzle materials, amplitude, measured chamber oxygen, mass yield and operating interruptions unresolved**. The cited 2023 predecessor may contain further information, but its full text was unavailable for verification. (uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 4-6, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 6-7, uhlmann2024acomparativeevaluation pages 15-15)

info.query:
Has anyone ultrasonically atomized nickel aluminum bronze or aluminum bronze (UNS C63000, C95800,
C95500, CuAl10Ni5Fe4, CuAl10Fe3 and similar), for example in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another
ultrasonic atomizer? For each report give the feedstock, melt temperature, crucible, nozzle and plate
(sonotrode) materials, frequency and amplitude, atmosphere and oxygen level, yield, particle size
distribution, morphology (satellites, flakes, irregular particles), oxygen content, and any problems
such as nozzle clogging, plate wear or interrupted flow. If there are none, give the closest
precedents: ultrasonic atomization of other aluminum-containing copper alloys, and gas atomization of
nickel aluminum bronze powder for laser powder-bed fusion or directed energy deposition.
